blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: How the economic activities that raise living standards may also pose threats to the natural environment and to people, locally and globally; why development has to be sustainable; and why conserving resources matters. A case study follows: a mining town where development left a risk still being managed.

blocks.heading: Threats at two scales
blocks.text: Economic development brings benefits - jobs, wages, roads and services - but the same activities may pose threats to the natural environment and to the people in it, and the threats work at two scales. Local threats damage a particular place: a river polluted below a works, a hillside eroded by overgrazing, the noise of a quarry over nearby homes. Global threats affect the whole planet, and enhanced global warming is the clearest case: carbon dioxide released anywhere mixes through the whole atmosphere, so the warming it drives is felt worldwide rather than beside the chimney that produced it. Pollution of one river is a local threat; the gas that drives global warming is a global one.

blocks.heading: Soil erosion and desertification
blocks.text: Farming that pushes land too hard removes the cover that protects the soil. Overcultivation grows crops on the same ground season after season until the fertility and the roots are gone; overgrazing lets herds eat the grass faster than it can regrow; the felling of trees takes away the roots and the shelter that hold soil together. Once bare ground is exposed, wind and rain remove the fertile topsoil - soil erosion - and in dry districts the loss can turn productive land into desert-like ground that supports neither crops nor herds: desertification. The people who feel it first are those who depend on the land: harvests thin out, grazing fails, and families drift towards the towns. Parts of southern Africa live with the threat.

blocks.heading: Enhanced global warming
blocks.text: Power stations, factories and vehicles burn fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - and each tonne burned releases carbon dioxide; cattle, rice growing and rotting waste add methane. These greenhouse gases trap some of the heat the Earth's surface radiates back towards space, and that natural greenhouse effect keeps the planet warm enough for life. The problem is the extra gas: human activity has thickened the trapping layer, so the atmosphere holds more heat - the enhanced greenhouse effect, usually called enhanced global warming. The consequences reach far: warming seas expand and ice on land melts, so low-lying coasts and deltas face rising seas, and heat and storms grow more extreme in some regions. Two cautions keep an answer accurate: the mechanism is heat trapped by gases, not the Sun burning hotter; and the greenhouse effect itself is natural - the enhancement by human activity is the risk.

blocks.heading: Pollution: name the kind
blocks.text: Pollution is the release into the environment of a substance or a form of energy that harms it or the people in it, and it comes in four kinds worth naming precisely. Water pollution: raw sewage, industrial waste and farm run-off released into rivers, lakes and the sea, which kills fish and threatens people who drink, wash and fish downstream. Air pollution: smoke and gases such as sulphur dioxide from burning fuel and smelting metal, which harms breathing. Noise pollution: traffic, machinery, aircraft and building works that disturb sleep and concentration. Visual pollution: the eyesores development can leave - derelict works, scrap heaps, pylons, litter. A precise answer names the threat: sulphur dioxide from the smelter, not "pollution"; soil erosion by wind and rain, not "the soil is damaged".

blocks.heading: Two errors to avoid
blocks.text: The first error mixes up two different problems: enhanced global warming and the thinning of the ozone layer are not the same thing. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat radiated from the Earth; a thinner ozone layer lets more ultraviolet light through. The test: is heat being trapped, or is ultraviolet being let in? The second error is vagueness: writing "pollution", "smoke" or "the environment is damaged" names nothing. A threat should carry its name - a gas such as sulphur dioxide, a water pollutant such as raw sewage, a process such as soil erosion by wind and rain.

blocks.heading: Sustainable development
blocks.text: Sustainable development is development that meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Development is needed, because people need jobs, food, homes and services now; but the way it is done can either keep or destroy tomorrow's ability to meet their own needs. A works that poisons a river has met some needs and taken others; a forest felled faster than it regrows pays this generation with the next generation's wood. Sustainability is a test applied to how development is done, not a rejection of it.

blocks.heading: A worked example: growth that had to be managed
blocks.text: Take Omatende, a coastal settlement of about 15 000 people that began drawing visitors for its beaches and birdlife. The growth brought guesthouses, a tarred road and boreholes - and three threats: sewage released into the lagoon, dune scrub cleared for plots, and woodfuel cut faster than the woodland regrew. Left alone, the development would eat the very things the visitors came for, so the town took three steps: waste water now passes through treatment beds before it reaches the lagoon; building is steered onto ground already cleared behind the shore, with the dune front planted rather than levelled; and woodland is cut on a rotation, with a village woodlot taking the fuel demand. The town still grows - but at a rate its surroundings can carry, which is the meaning of sustainable management.

blocks.heading: Sustainable does not mean building more
blocks.text: A common error treats sustainable development as a licence for more building: more hotels, bigger works, wider roads. The definition points the opposite way: a plan that builds without limit can exhaust the very resource it depends on, and the test of sustainability is whether that resource will still be there for the next generation. The reef under a capped number of divers passes the test; the same reef under a plan to double visitor numbers does not, because the reef, not the building, is what the visitors came for.

blocks.heading: Resource conservation
blocks.text: Resource conservation means using resources carefully so that they last. Renewable resources - fish stocks, forests, water, soil - can replace what is taken provided they are harvested no faster than they renew, so conserving them means quotas, replanting and rotation. Non-renewable resources - minerals and fossil fuels - cannot be replaced within a human lifetime, so conserving them means stretching the supply: using them efficiently, reusing what has been won once, and recycling what would otherwise be dumped, so less needs to be mined and felled fresh.

blocks.heading: Why conservation matters
blocks.text: Conservation matters because overuse can destroy resources together with the livelihoods resting on them. An overfished lake can take decades to recover; a woodland cleared for fuel exposes its soil to erosion and shortens the firewood supply in the same act; a town that wastes part of its piped water reaches its supply limit sooner. Less mining, felling, manufacturing and dumping also means less pollution and fewer of the emissions that drive enhanced global warming. Conserved resources keep serving the next generation; squandered ones leave the bill with people who did not spend them.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The development that raises the risks is measured in topic 3.1; farming that erodes soil in 3.2; industry's wastes in 3.3 and tourism's footprints in 3.4; energy choices in 3.5; water supply and pollution in 3.6. Topic 5's fieldwork can measure one of these threats at first hand.
